title: Double `/`, `//`, `%` by a scalar: a multiplication by the reciprocal
verdict: `divide` of doubles by a scalar rounds twice (2u, `approx`) and overflows below the smallest normal divisor; `//` and `%` give wrong results
description: With a length-1 divisor (a literal) against a column of two or more rows, Polars's in-memory engine computes `x / c` as `x * (1 / c)`: `49.0 / 49.0` is `0.9999999999999999`, and `0.0 / 1e-310` is NaN (`1 / 1e-310` is `inf`, and `0 * inf` NaN). `//` and `%` divide the same way. A column divisor of the same length divides as IEEE does. Here the streaming engine gave the IEEE quotient on four rows, because a frame shorter than the thread count streams as one-row morsels; on longer frames, or on one thread, streaming takes the reciprocal too (polars-double-scalar-divisor, PL-3).

The same finding as polars-double-scalar-divisor (PL-3), which carries the source reading, the streaming probes (the reciprocal path also runs on streaming once a morsel holds two or more rows: `s-scalar-divisor`, 9,000 rows) and the ulp bound (polars-ulp-arith). This fact keeps its id for the engine tables (`SubstraitLean/EngineTables.lean`) that cite it.
reference: `divide` of doubles rounds the exact quotient once (`TIE_TO_EVEN`), and `0.0 / c` is `0.0` for a finite nonzero `c`. Decided on #444: Polars's `/` is `approx` with 2u per division, under the precondition that a divisor is 0 or not subnormal; `//` and `%` floor the quotient (`49.0 % 49.0` is `49.0`), so their translation broadcasts the divisor to a column (`column_divisor`).
